title: Microorganisms & Biotechnology
description: An introduction to bacteria, viruses, fungi, and protozoa; their useful roles in food, medicine, and bioremediation; how pathogens cause disease; and the aseptic techniques used to culture microbes safely.

notes.heading: 📌 Definition: The Four Main Types of Microorganisms
notes.body:
Microorganisms (microbes) are living organisms too small to see with the naked eye. They are found almost everywhere on Earth. The four main groups studied in MYP biology are:

1. Bacteria — single-celled prokaryotes with no membrane-bound nucleus. Many are harmless or beneficial; a few can cause disease. Shape examples include rods (bacilli), spheres (cocci), and spirals (spirilla).

2. Viruses — not cells at all; they are tiny particles made of genetic material (DNA or RNA) inside a protein coat. They cannot reproduce on their own — they must infect a host cell and hijack its machinery.

3. Fungi — eukaryotes that include single-celled yeasts and multicellular moulds and mushrooms. They feed by secreting enzymes onto organic matter and absorbing the nutrients.

4. Protozoa (protists) — single-celled eukaryotes, many of which can move using flagella, cilia, or pseudopodia. Some are parasites that cause disease.

illustration.alt: Diagram showing the four main types of microorganisms and examples of their useful and harmful roles.
illustration.caption: Bacteria, viruses, fungi, and protozoa each have distinctive structures and roles in ecosystems, biotechnology, and disease.

notes.heading: 🔑 How It Works: Microorganisms in Food — Yoghurt and Bread
notes.body:
Many foods depend on microbes to develop flavour, texture, or shelf life. Two classic examples are:

Yoghurt: Milk is heated to kill unwanted microbes, then cooled. Beneficial bacteria such as Lactobacillus are added. These bacteria ferment lactose (milk sugar) into lactic acid. The lactic acid lowers the pH, causing milk proteins to curdle and thicken into yoghurt. The acid also helps preserve the food by inhibiting the growth of spoilage bacteria.

Bread: Baker's yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) is a single-celled fungus. When mixed with flour and water, yeast carries out anaerobic respiration (fermentation), breaking down sugars to produce carbon dioxide and ethanol. The carbon dioxide gas becomes trapped in the dough, making it rise and creating the airy texture of bread. The ethanol evaporates during baking.

illustration.alt: Diagram showing the four main types of microorganisms and examples of their useful and harmful roles.
illustration.caption: Lactic acid bacteria thicken milk into yoghurt; yeast produces carbon dioxide that makes bread dough rise.

notes.heading: 🔑 Key Concept: Microorganisms in Medicine and Biotechnology
notes.body:
Microbes are essential tools in modern medicine and biotechnology. Important examples include:

• Antibiotics: Many antibiotics are naturally produced by fungi or bacteria. Penicillin, the first widely used antibiotic, is made by the fungus Penicillium. It kills bacteria by disrupting their cell walls. Antibiotics do NOT work on viruses.

• Insulin production: Genetically modified bacteria are used to produce human insulin for people with diabetes. The human insulin gene is inserted into bacterial DNA; the bacteria multiply and produce insulin as they grow.

• Vaccines: Some vaccines use weakened or inactivated viruses or bacteria (or parts of them) to train the immune system without causing disease.

• Enzymes and vitamins: Bacteria and fungi are used to manufacture enzymes for washing powders, food processing, and vitamin supplements such as vitamin B12.

illustration.alt: Diagram showing the four main types of microorganisms and examples of their useful and harmful roles.
illustration.caption: Penicillium fungus produces penicillin, and genetically modified bacteria can produce medicines such as insulin.

notes.heading: 💡 Worked Example: Biogas Production
notes.body:
Biogas is a renewable fuel produced when microorganisms break down organic waste without oxygen. This process is called anaerobic digestion.

Worked example — how a simple biogas generator works:

1. Organic material (such as animal manure, food waste, or sewage sludge) is placed in a sealed, airtight digester.
2. The mixture is kept warm (around 35–55 °C) and stirred to help the microbes work efficiently.
3. Anaerobic bacteria and archaea digest the waste, producing a mixture of gases.
4. The main product is methane (CH₄), which can be burned as a fuel for cooking, heating, or generating electricity.
5. A by-product is digestate — a nutrient-rich residue used as fertiliser.

This process is useful because it reduces waste, produces renewable energy, and returns nutrients to the soil.

illustration.alt: Diagram showing the four main types of microorganisms and examples of their useful and harmful roles.
illustration.caption: Anaerobic digesters use microorganisms to convert organic waste into methane-rich biogas.

notes.heading: 📎 Key Points to Remember: Pathogens and Disease Prevention
notes.body:
A pathogen is a microorganism that can cause disease. Pathogens can be bacteria, viruses, fungi, or protozoa. Important examples to remember:

• Bacterial diseases: tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis), cholera (Vibrio cholerae), Salmonella food poisoning, dental plaque.
• Viral diseases: influenza (flu), common cold, measles, COVID-19, HIV/AIDS.
• Fungal diseases: athlete's foot, ringworm, thrush.
• Protozoan diseases: malaria (Plasmodium, spread by mosquitoes), amoebic dysentery.

Disease prevention methods include:

• Personal hygiene — handwashing with soap removes many pathogens.
• Safe food handling — cooking food thoroughly and storing it correctly.
• Clean water supply — preventing waterborne diseases such as cholera.
• Vaccination — stimulating immunity before infection.
• Vector control — reducing mosquito populations to limit malaria spread.
• Using barriers — condoms reduce sexually transmitted infections; masks reduce airborne transmission.

illustration.alt: Diagram showing the four main types of microorganisms and examples of their useful and harmful roles.
illustration.caption: Pathogens cause disease through many routes; hygiene, vaccination, and vector control all reduce transmission.

notes.heading: ⚠️ Common Mistake: Aseptic Technique
notes.body:
Aseptic technique is a set of practices used to prevent unwanted microorganisms from contaminating cultures — and to prevent cultured microbes from escaping into the environment. It is NOT the same as sterilisation alone; it includes a combination of methods used throughout an experiment.

Key steps:

• Sterilise equipment and work surfaces before starting (e.g., with disinfectant or autoclaving).
• Pass the neck of culture bottles through a Bunsen burner flame before and after pouring or transferring — the hot air creates an updraft that keeps airborne contaminants away.
• Work near a lit Bunsen burner when transferring cultures; the rising hot air reduces the chance of falling contaminants landing in the Petri dish.
• Use sterile loops, pipettes, and spreaders for each transfer.
• Seal Petri dishes with tape and incubate them upside down so condensation does not drip onto the agar surface.
• Incubate at around 25 °C in school laboratories — NOT 37 °C, which is close to human body temperature and could encourage the growth of harmful human pathogens.
• Dispose of cultures safely by autoclaving; never open used plates.

illustration.alt: Diagram showing the four main types of microorganisms and examples of their useful and harmful roles.
illustration.caption: Aseptic technique keeps cultures pure and prevents the release of potentially harmful microorganisms.

notes.heading: ✅ Check: Useful vs Harmful Microorganisms — Summary
notes.body:
Microorganisms can be useful or harmful depending on the species and situation.

Useful roles:
• Decomposers — break down dead organisms and recycle nutrients in ecosystems.
• Nitrogen fixation — some soil bacteria convert atmospheric nitrogen into forms plants can use.
• Food production — yoghurt, cheese, bread, vinegar, alcohol, and soy sauce all rely on microbes.
• Biotechnology — producing antibiotics, insulin, enzymes, and biofuels such as biogas.
• Bioremediation — using microbes to clean up pollutants such as oil spills or industrial waste.

Harmful roles:
• Disease — pathogens cause infections in plants, animals, and humans.
• Food spoilage — moulds and bacteria can rot food, making it unsafe to eat.
• Crop damage — some fungi and bacteria cause plant diseases, reducing food production.

Remember: whether a microbe is 'good' or 'bad' depends on where it is, what it is doing, and how it interacts with its host or environment.

illustration.alt: Diagram showing the four main types of microorganisms and examples of their useful and harmful roles.
illustration.caption: The same group of organisms can be helpful in one context and harmful in another.

flashcards.definition: Single-celled prokaryotic microorganisms with no membrane-bound nucleus. They can be spherical, rod-shaped, or spiral.
flashcards.example: Lactobacillus bacteria are used to make yoghurt by fermenting lactose into lactic acid.

flashcards.definition: A tiny infectious particle made of genetic material inside a protein coat. Viruses cannot reproduce independently; they must infect a host cell.
flashcards.example: The influenza virus infects human respiratory cells, causing flu symptoms.

flashcards.definition: Eukaryotic organisms that include yeasts, moulds, and mushrooms. They digest food externally and absorb nutrients.
flashcards.example: Yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) ferments sugars to produce carbon dioxide, which makes bread dough rise.

flashcards.definition: Single-celled eukaryotic organisms, many of which can move and some of which are parasites that cause disease.
flashcards.example: Plasmodium is a protozoan parasite transmitted by mosquitoes; it can cause malaria.

flashcards.definition: A microorganism that can cause disease in its host. Pathogens include harmful bacteria, viruses, fungi, and protozoa.
flashcards.example: Salmonella bacteria are pathogens that can cause food poisoning if contaminated food is eaten.

flashcards.definition: A set of laboratory practices used to prevent contamination of microbial cultures and to stop cultured microbes from escaping.
flashcards.example: Flaming the neck of a culture bottle and working near a Bunsen burner flame both help maintain aseptic conditions.

flashcards.definition: An anaerobic process in which microorganisms break down sugars to produce useful products such as acids, alcohol, or gases.
flashcards.example: In bread making, yeast fermentation produces carbon dioxide gas that causes dough to rise.

flashcards.definition: A type of fermentation carried out by bacteria in which sugars are converted into lactic acid.
flashcards.example: Lactobacillus converts lactose in milk into lactic acid, thickening the milk into yoghurt.

flashcards.definition: A renewable fuel, mainly methane, produced by microorganisms breaking down organic waste in the absence of oxygen.
flashcards.example: Anaerobic digesters use animal manure and food waste to produce methane for cooking or electricity generation.

flashcards.definition: The use of living organisms, usually microorganisms, to break down or remove pollutants from the environment.
flashcards.example: Certain bacteria can digest oil hydrocarbons, helping to clean up oil spills.

flashcards.definition: A substance produced by or derived from microorganisms that kills or inhibits the growth of bacteria.
flashcards.example: Penicillin is an antibiotic produced by the fungus Penicillium; it disrupts bacterial cell walls.

flashcards.definition: The process of inserting a gene from one organism into a microorganism so that the microbe produces a useful substance.
flashcards.example: Bacteria can be genetically modified with the human insulin gene to produce insulin for treating diabetes.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a single-celled prokaryote with no membrane-bound nucleus?
questions.explanation: Bacteria are prokaryotes — their DNA is not enclosed in a nucleus. Fungi and protozoa are eukaryotes, and viruses are not cells at all.

questions.stem: Which gas does yeast produce during bread making that makes the dough rise?
questions.explanation: Yeast ferments sugars anaerobically to produce carbon dioxide and ethanol. The carbon dioxide gas becomes trapped in the dough, causing it to rise.

questions.stem: In yoghurt production, what substance do bacteria such as Lactobacillus produce from lactose?
questions.explanation: Lactic acid bacteria ferment lactose into lactic acid, which lowers pH and causes milk proteins to curdle into yoghurt.

questions.stem: Which type of microorganism is used to produce penicillin, an antibiotic that kills bacteria?
questions.explanation: Penicillin was originally discovered in the fungus Penicillium. It works by interfering with bacterial cell wall formation.

questions.stem: Why are antibiotics NOT effective against viral infections such as the common cold?
choices: Viruses are too large for antibiotics to enter
Antibiotics target bacterial structures such as cell walls and ribosomes, which viruses do not have
Viruses reproduce too slowly for antibiotics to work
Antibiotics only work in acidic environments
questions.explanation: Viruses lack the cellular structures that antibiotics attack, such as cell walls and bacterial ribosomes. They also replicate inside host cells.

questions.stem: Which disease is caused by a protozoan parasite transmitted through mosquito bites?
questions.explanation: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium, a protozoan parasite transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes. The other options are caused by a virus, fungus, and bacterium respectively.

questions.stem: What is the main useful product of anaerobic digestion in a biogas generator?
questions.explanation: Anaerobic microorganisms digest organic waste and release methane-rich biogas, which can be burned as a renewable fuel.

choices: Using microbes to clean up environmental pollutants
Using chemicals to kill all soil microorganisms
Removing bacteria from drinking water by boiling
questions.explanation: Bioremediation uses microorganisms to break down or remove pollutants such as oil, heavy metals, or industrial chemicals from the environment.

questions.stem: Which of these is the main reason school microbiology cultures are incubated at about 25 °C rather than 37 °C?
choices: 37 °C is close to human body temperature and could encourage the growth of harmful human pathogens
questions.explanation: Incubating at 25 °C allows safe bacterial species to grow while reducing the risk of culturing pathogens adapted to the human body.

questions.stem: Which statement about viruses is correct?
choices: Viruses can reproduce independently in nutrient broth
Viruses must enter a host cell to replicate
Viruses have cell walls made of cellulose
questions.explanation: Viruses are not cells and cannot carry out life processes on their own. They must infect a host cell and hijack its machinery to reproduce.

questions.stem: Which microorganism is commonly used in genetic modification to produce human insulin?
questions.explanation: The human insulin gene is inserted into bacteria such as E. coli, which then multiply and produce human insulin as they grow.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a correct match between a microorganism and a food product it helps make?
questions.explanation: Lactobacillus bacteria ferment lactose into lactic acid to make yoghurt. Yeast is used in bread, and biogas is produced by anaerobic microbes digesting waste.

questions.stem: Why is aseptic technique important when transferring bacteria onto an agar plate?
choices: It makes the bacteria grow faster
It prevents unwanted microorganisms from contaminating the culture and reduces the escape of cultured microbes
It increases the nutrient content of the agar
It kills all the bacteria instantly
questions.explanation: Aseptic technique protects both the experiment (keeping the culture pure) and the environment (preventing potentially harmful microbes from escaping).

questions.stem: Which disease is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis?
questions.explanation: Tuberculosis (TB) is a bacterial disease affecting the lungs. Malaria is protozoan, while influenza and COVID-19 are viral.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of a useful role of microorganisms in ecosystems?
choices: Breaking down dead organisms and recycling nutrients
questions.explanation: As decomposers, microorganisms break down dead organic matter and release nutrients back into the soil, supporting plant growth and nutrient cycling.
